note: Checked Nov 22. Every item was read at its source. Items marked Verify have a detail that still needs confirming with the funder. Nothing is included just to fill space.

items.title: Atlanta Public Schools holds community conversation on AI policy for students and parents
items.why: A metro district is publicly debating student AI rules. Districts nearby will likely follow, so frame your classes as teacher-guided, objective-based AI literacy with no sensitive student data entered, and offer that language to Newton, Rockdale and Clayton decision makers.

items.title: APS proposed AI rules: students may use AI only for a stated instructional objective, staff keep sensitive data out
items.why: Borrow this framing word for word in emails: objective-based, teacher-guided, no sensitive data entered. APS planned to decide at a November meeting, so check whether it passed before you call it adopted.

items.title: Georgia students raise privacy concerns over Meta AI smart glasses; state law bans such devices in schools
items.why: Student privacy and recording are live issues with Georgia families and schools. Add a short data-privacy and device-use statement to your program overview so administrators see you are ahead of the concern.

items.title: Teachers say district AI rules are unclear: 60% of educators disagree their district made policy clear (EdWeek 2025 figure cited)
items.why: Offer teacher training next to student classes: using AI safely, protecting student data, checking AI output. Raise it with Dr. Williams after InspiHER.

items.title: Georgia colleges add mandatory AI coursework while worrying students over-rely on AI
items.why: Colleges now require AI classes and stress critical thinking over tool use. Use this in pitches: your program builds the thinking skills and basic AI literacy students need before college.

items.title: Toshiba America Foundation: grades 6-12 STEM project grants
items.why: Teachers apply, you supply the project. Send to your NCSA and NCCA contacts: a teacher can request funds to bring you in.
items.who: Grade 6-12 educators (not stated for schools or nonprofits)
items.verify: Listing gives Nov 1 and Dec 1, 2026 without saying which tier. Check the funder page.

items.title: BOOST out-of-school-time grants: $7.5M expansion announced May 18, 2026
items.why: BOOST pays community after-school groups, and it has funded STEM supplies and staff training. Ask every after-school prospect: are you a BOOST grantee, and can it cover a vendor like us?
items.amount: Last cycle: $20K-$300K a year for community groups
items.who: Georgia nonprofits, municipalities and colleges serving public K-12 students in after-school or summer programs (2+ years, 25%+ low-income)
items.verify: Next application window not announced. Last cycle closed Aug 1, 2025. Watch afterschoolga.org.

items.title: Education Department now favors grant proposals that build AI literacy and teach educators to use AI
items.why: Districts and colleges that propose AI literacy and teacher training score higher on federal discretionary grants. Offer Newton, Rockdale, Clayton or Gwinnett a co-written application: you bring the curriculum and training.
items.who: Districts and colleges (article does not mention nonprofits)
items.verify: Final rule effective May 13, 2026. It names no specific grant programs.

items.title: Georgia 21st Century Community Learning Centers (after-school funding)
items.why: The biggest after-school funding stream in the state, so many of your prospects depend on it. Federal money for Georgia was frozen then restored in July 2025, so ask prospects how secure theirs is.
items.verify: Current Georgia application dates not confirmed. Check GaDOE before you tell anyone a deadline.

items.title: Gwinnett County identified $18M in administrative costs it could cut
items.why: Gwinnett is already planning for tighter budgets. Pitch your classes as low cost and grant-fundable, and send the Gwinnett email in that frame.

items.title: House committee advanced a FY2027 plan to cut Title I by $1.6B and end over $3B in teacher training and English-learner grants
items.why: If this passes, districts lose teacher-training money. Do not build your plan on district PD budgets. After-school and community funders are steadier ground.
items.verify: Senate had not acted as of June 2026.

items.title: BOOST statewide grantees: Georgia Alliance of Boys & Girls Clubs ($2M), Georgia Alliance of YMCAs ($1.8M), Georgia Recreation and Park Association ($1.6M)
items.why: These groups pass funding to local sites. You already have Newton Boys & Girls Club and Heritage Hills. Add your local YMCA branches and county parks and recreation department as new prospects.
